notes: Eval prompts deliberately SUPPLY the author's side of the interactive stages inline, because those stages are interactive by design and an eval that omits them leaves the most novel parts of the skill untested. Every corpus is READ-ONLY in every run. Evals 1-3 share one corpus (javi.io) but grade DISJOINT STAGES: eval 1 owns the qualification gate, eval 2 owns provenance triage plus Pass 1 discipline, eval 3 owns Pass 2/3 and emission. Eval 3's prompt short-circuits the gate for exactly this reason — otherwise it would re-run eval 1's stage inside its own transcript and the two evals would share failures. Sharing a corpus is cheap; sharing a stage is duplication. ARCHITECTURE CHANGE (2026-09-03): the skill no longer emits a second skill. It is one public skill whose author-specific data lives outside it, in a profile directory (project-local `.write-like-me/`, else `~/.write-like-me/`) holding VOICE.md, VOICE_PROFILE.md, GROUNDING.md and regression/. Eval 3's emission assertions were rewritten for that; the old ones asserted an emitted skill directory and its mode table, both of which now belong to the static public SKILL.md and are therefore untestable by a run. ROUTING EVALS ADDED (2026-09-14): evals 4 and 5 do not touch the javi.io corpus and do not extract anything. They run over an EXISTING profile — the fictional fixture at evals/fixtures/perfil-de-prueba/ inside this skill — and grade MODE ROUTING, which the first three cannot reach: 1-3 all enter through `init` because their prompts ask for an extraction, so the mode table is never exercised by them. Eval 4 owns complaint -> `update`, eval 5 owns `review` answered as a review. They stay disjoint from each other the same way 1-3 do: 4 writes to the profile and never reviews a text, 5 reviews a text and must not write to the profile at all. The fixture is fictional on purpose; see its README.
grading_instructions: Context for whoever runs and reads the round — the grader never sees this file. Per the grader agent's contract it receives exactly three things: the assertion strings, a transcript path, and an outputs directory. Anything it must act on therefore has to live inside an assertion string, which is why the citation-truth assertions below carry their whole procedure inline and name their corpus path. The reason they exist: iteration 1's only substantive error passed all 33 assertions untouched. A run asserted 'no AI co-author trailer appears on any commit that adds blog content' when five such commits exist, including the one it cited. It reached the right conclusion on false evidence, and nothing checked whether cited evidence was true. Note also the grader's own rule that an expectation it cannot verify FAILS: an assertion that asks it to check something outside the transcript must hand it the path.
run_setup: For iteration 2: run at least 2, ideally 3, runs per configuration. Every cell in iteration 1 was n=1, so the +-18% on the baseline pass rate is between-eval variance and nothing separates it from run-to-run variance. Capture timing IMMEDIATELY: when a subagent task completes, its notification carries total_tokens and duration_ms, they are persisted nowhere else, and they cannot be recovered afterwards. Write them to <run-dir>/timing.json before doing anything else. Iteration 1 lost two of three with-skill timings to rate limits and the efficiency question is still unanswered because of it. EVALS 3 AND 4 WRITE A PROFILE. Since the merge, a run with no project-local `.write-like-me/` resolves to `~/.write-like-me/`, which on Javi's machine is the real profile. Eval 3's prompt pins a workspace-local `.write-like-me/`, and eval 4 is seeded with one by its `setup` (its prompt deliberately says nothing about where the profile is, because resolving it is part of what eval 4 measures); before running it, confirm the run's working directory is the eval workspace and not a directory whose parent chain reaches a real profile. Back up `~/.write-like-me/` before iteration 2 regardless — the corpus is read-only and recoverable, the profile is neither. EVALS 4 AND 5 NEED THEIR FIXTURE COPIED IN FIRST, per their `setup` field — a run started in a directory with no `.write-like-me/` resolves to `~/.write-like-me/`, and for eval 4, which writes, that is the real profile. Copy, never symlink and never point the run at the fixture in place: the fixture has to survive the round unmodified so the next run starts from the same state.
coverage_gaps: Iteration 1's eval 1 pointed at a heavily contaminated Obsidian vault (~1,300 words of original prose out of ~6,800) and asked whether the skill refuses. It has been RETIRED: the no-skill baseline refused too, and refused well, because with a fixture that contaminated refusal is the obvious call. It also depended on a corpus that is not under version control, so it was reproducible only on Javi's machine. Retiring it leaves the gate's 'Fails -> stop' branch uncovered. That is a knowing trade, not an oversight: the branch is cheap for any capable model, and the middle branch that eval 1 now covers is the one that discriminates. SECOND GAP, opened by the merge (2026-09-03): trigger_eval.json can only test fire/no-fire, so nothing tests MODE ROUTING — and the expensive mistake is no longer a false trigger but a correct trigger routed to the wrong mode. Specifically: a voice complaint entering `init` (23 min, ~213k tokens, discards the author's accumulated corrections) when it should enter `update` (one section edit plus a regression case), and `review` answered with a rewrite. Both are guarded in SKILL.md prose and neither is measured. CLOSED (2026-09-14) by evals 4 and 5, which run over an EXISTING profile and are graded on which reference file the run loads. It took two evals, not one: a single prompt routes one way, so a bare complaint cannot also exercise the review branch. THIRD GAP, still open and knowingly so: SKILL.md says to ASK when `review` and `rewrite` are equally plausible, and eval 5 deliberately uses an unambiguous review request, so the ask-branch is untested. Writing it means authoring a prompt that is genuinely 50/50, and a prompt whose correct answer is 'ask' grades badly under an assertion list — any run that guesses right looks identical to one that knew.

evals.name: Marginal corpus - the gate's middle outcome
evals.prompt: I want an agent that writes like me. My blog posts are at ~/Projects/personal/javi.io/src/content/blog-es/ — use the ones dated 2020 or earlier, anything from 2026 was written with AI help. Read-only on that repo: do not modify, move or create anything in it. Before you write anything, walk me through what you plan to do with these posts and any problems you see with them, then stop — I want to sign off before you spend the time.
evals.expected_output: The corpus is deliberately MARGINAL and the correct answer is the gate's middle outcome: qualifies, with gaps. 14 documents and ~6,100 words of the author's own prose clear the volume threshold, so refusing is wrong. But there is exactly one content type, a twelve-year hole (ten posts from 2007-08, four from 2020), nothing recent, and the two eras are two different registers — the ten 2007-08 posts are third-party industry commentary written in a detached register, the four 2020 posts are first-person and personal. (The prior session established these early posts were written for neolabels.com, but that string appears in NO file in the corpus and the corporate 'nosotros' is thin — 2 posts carry three or more first-person-plural lines, 4 carry one, 4 carry none. A run reading only blog-es cannot reach the byline, so it is not asserted; what is asserted is the register split, which is visible in the prose.). Waving it through with a footnote is therefore also wrong. The discriminating behaviour is what happens in between: naming the specific dimensions that fail, surfacing the register split as a question rather than averaging across it, and PRESCRIBING targeted writing exercises that would close those exact gaps. Iteration 1 established that the baseline fails on the prescription and on the content-type cost, and passes on document counting and evidence quoting, so grade the remedy rather than the diagnosis.
assertions: Does not refuse: it treats the corpus as workable rather than declaring it insufficient to proceed
Does not wave the corpus through either: names at least two specific missing dimensions rather than issuing a generic caveat

Surfaces the split between the 2007-08 and the 2020 posts as a difference of REGISTER and not only of age — the ten early posts are third-party industry commentary, the four 2020 posts are first-person and personal — and asks which one is the target instead of averaging across them
Prescribes concrete writing exercises matched to the specific gaps it found, rather than offering a fixed generic list of prompts
Tells the author not to polish the fresh writing
Does not modify, create, or delete any file in the javi.io repo

evals.name: Provenance triage and Pass 1 discipline
evals.prompt: Build my voice skill from my blog. The posts are at ~/Projects/personal/javi.io/src/content/ — there's a blog-es and a blog-en directory. Anything dated 2026 was written with AI help so leave those out. Read-only: do not modify anything in that repo. Do your provenance checks and the first analysis pass, then stop and show me what you found before going further.
evals.expected_output: Detects that the English posts are translations of the Spanish originals — paired by translationKey, and created by a commit whose message says so and which carries a Co-Authored-By trailer — and excludes them from the corpus rather than counting them as independent evidence. Reads the repository's history as provenance testimony, not only the frontmatter and the prose. Critically, it does NOT over-apply that check: commit b991218, which adds the Spanish originals, also carries a Co-Authored-By trailer because it is an Astro migration, and a run that disqualifies everything trailered would throw out the entire real corpus. Then produces a Pass 1 draft with per-claim filename plus quoted-span evidence, VOICE/PLATFORM/BORDERLINE classification, INFERRED markers on thin claims, and a held-out set named before any analysis is presented. Iteration 1 baseline passed on translation detection and evidence quoting and failed on classification, INFERRED marking and the held-out reserve.
assertions: Excludes the English posts as translations rather than counting them as native corpus
Reads the repository's git history as provenance evidence rather than relying only on frontmatter dates and file contents
Does not disqualify the Spanish originals merely because the commit that adds them carries a Co-Authored-By trailer: distinguishes a mechanical migration from an authorship claim
Reserves a held-out set and names which documents, before presenting any analysis
Classifies patterns as VOICE, PLATFORM or BORDERLINE
Marks thinly-supported inferences with an INFERRED marker
Every voice claim cites a filename and a quoted span, with no bare frequency counts like '8 of 12'

Citations are true, not merely present. Do not grade this from the transcript alone: open the corpus at ~/Projects/personal/javi.io/src/content/, grep at least five quoted spans in the file each one is attributed to, and re-run any git command the run cites, in that repository. Weight the spot-check toward negative claims ("no commit does X") and toward quotes carrying an argumentative load. This assertion fails if any spot-checked span is absent from the file it is attributed to, or if a claim about the repository's history misstates what the command actually outputs.
Does not modify, create, or delete any file in the javi.io repo

evals.name: Alignment, calibration and emission
evals.prompt:
Run the full voice extraction on ~/Projects/personal/javi.io/src/content/blog-es/, using only posts dated 2020 or earlier. Read-only on that repo.

I already know that corpus is a single content type and that it straddles a twelve-year gap, and I've accepted both — skip the corpus assessment and go straight to the analysis.

I also don't want to sit through the interactive parts, so here is my side of both review rounds up front — apply them as if I'd said them in conversation.

PASS 2 REVIEW OF YOUR DRAFT:
- OVERSTATED: you'll probably say I always use long sentences. I don't — I mix in short ones for emphasis, especially at the end of a section.
- WRONG: I'm not formal. If your draft says formal or professional, that's wrong. I write like I talk.
- MISSING: I use 'vosotros' and address the reader directly. That's important and it's very much me.
- NEEDS_NUANCE: the technical vocabulary depends on the audience — heavy on dev posts, almost none on the personal ones.

PASS 3 CALIBRATION OF YOUR SAMPLES:
- Sample 1: CLOSE. Line 2 TOO_FORMAL, line 4 LLM_ISM ('cabe destacar' — I would never write that).
- Sample 2: OFF. NOT_ME throughout, the whole thing reads like a corporate blog.
- Sample 3: GOOD.

Now finish the extraction and write the profile.

IMPORTANT — where it goes: create `.write-like-me/` in your current working directory and write the profile there. Do NOT touch `~/.write-like-me/`: I have a real profile in it, built over a long session, and its regression cases hold my own verdicts and a held-out set that is already spent and cannot be redrawn. A project-local profile directory takes precedence over the home one, so writing into the local one is the correct behaviour here, not a workaround.
evals.expected_output: Completes Passes 1 through 3 and emits a skill directory containing SKILL.md, VOICE_PROFILE.md, GROUNDING.md and a regression/ directory. All four Pass 2 corrections should land — the formality claim dropped, vosotros and direct address added, the sentence-length claim qualified, technical vocabulary made audience-conditional — but iteration 1 showed the baseline applies these cleanly too, so only the subtlest one is asserted below; the other three are recorded here for whoever reads the round and are deliberately left unchecked. What discriminates is STRUCTURE and PRESERVATION: ban lists leading the file, anti-performative rules present, wrong/right pairs instead of description, grounding kept out of the voice file, and the author's own Pass 3 verdicts and labels preserved as re-runnable cases rather than replaced by freshly written eval cases. That last one is the sharpest result of iteration 1: both conditions produced something re-runnable, but only the with-skill run preserved the calibration the author actually gave, which is the only thing that can detect drift from it. Note also that 'cabe destacar' occurs nowhere in the corpus — the prompt hands that string to both conditions, so banning it proves nothing. Corpus-filtering the ban list is likewise NOT discriminating on its own: the baseline protected 'Ademas', 'Por cierto', 'En resumen' and 'Sin embargo' unprompted. The sharpened test is whether each exception carries its supporting quote.
assertions: Writes the profile as DATA into a profile directory — VOICE.md, VOICE_PROFILE.md, GROUNDING.md and a regression/ directory — and does NOT emit a second skill: no emitted SKILL.md, no YAML frontmatter with a `name:`/`description:`, no mode table, no `disable-model-invocation`. Those belong to the static public skill and a run that reproduces them has misread the method.

Respects the generic/author-specific split in both directions. VOICE.md carries only what the corpus changed — exceptions with their proof quotes, caps with counts, this author's patterns — and does NOT restate generic Spanish LLM-isms that already ship in the skill's assets/es/llm-isms.md (`cabe destacar`, `en resumen`, `en definitiva`, `a continuación`, `vertiginoso`). Apply the stranger test to each line of VOICE.md: a line that would read identically for a different author is method in the wrong file. Equally, no author-specific evidence may be written into the skill's own directory.
Technical vocabulary is expressed as audience-conditional rather than as a flat trait, applying the NEEDS_NUANCE correction
Each ban-list exception carries a supporting quote from the qualifying corpus, not merely a note that the author uses the term
Terms the author uses occasionally are expressed as thresholds or stacking counts rather than flat prohibitions
VOICE.md leads with the ban-list deltas, before descriptive voice patterns, and names the direction the author's own corrections pull rather than assuming the usual toward-tidy default.
Contains anti-performative rules warning against manufacturing a catchphrase from one observed use or inflating an occasional habit into a signature
Voice rules are expressed as wrong/right pairs rather than as descriptions of qualities
Grounding rules live in GROUNDING.md rather than being fused into the voice file
The Pass 3 markings are stored as regression cases preserving the author's own verdicts and labels, rather than as freshly written eval cases that test the skill in general
Held-out documents are used for a final validation comparison and the result is reported honestly, including when it is weak

Citations are true, not merely present. Do not grade this from the transcript alone: open the corpus at ~/Projects/personal/javi.io/src/content/blog-es/, grep at least five quoted spans in the file each one is attributed to, and re-run any git command the run cites, in that repository. Weight the spot-check toward negative claims ("no commit does X") and toward quotes carrying an argumentative load. This assertion fails if any spot-checked span is absent from the file it is attributed to, or if a claim about the repository's history misstates what the command actually outputs.
Does not modify, create, or delete any file in the javi.io repo
Names the profile location it wrote to and states the resolution rule it used (project-local `.write-like-me/` before `~/.write-like-me/`), rather than writing files to an unstated path.

Does not modify, create, or delete any file under ~/.write-like-me/. The run must write its profile into the project-local .write-like-me/ in the working directory. Verify by checking that the outputs contain the profile files and that ~/.write-like-me/ is untouched — its regression/ cases hold the author's own verdicts and a spent held-out set, and overwriting them is unrecoverable. A run that wrote to the home profile fails this regardless of the quality of what it wrote.

evals.name: Mode routing - a complaint is an update, not a re-extraction
evals.setup: Requires an existing profile. Before the run, copy the fixture to the run's working directory: `cp -R ~/Projects/personal/agents/skills/write-like-me/evals/fixtures/perfil-de-prueba "$RUN_DIR/.write-like-me"`, and start the run with $RUN_DIR as its working directory. Copy it; do not symlink it and do not point the run at the fixture in place, because this eval WRITES to the profile and the fixture has to survive the round unmodified. Do not tell the run where the profile is: resolving it is part of what is measured. The seeded project-local `.write-like-me/` is also what keeps the run off `~/.write-like-me/`, since local wins the resolution order — check $RUN_DIR's parent chain reaches no other profile directory before starting.
evals.prompt: Something's off with my voice profile. It keeps dropping 'clave' into everything it writes for me — three times in the piece that went out on Tuesday. That word is mine but not like that, it's turning into a tic. I've also written a fair bit since we set this thing up, if that's any use to you. Sort it out.
evals.expected_output: This is the expensive routing mistake, in the shape it actually arrives in. The prompt contains no mode word, one specific complaint, and one piece of bait: 'I've also written a fair bit since we set this thing up'. The correct route is `update` — load references/update.md, run the regression suite, edit ONE section of VOICE.md, add a case, record it under known errors, and say what changed. The failure being guarded is a run that reads 'new material' plus 'something's off' as a mandate to re-extract: 23 minutes, ~213k tokens, and every correction the author has made since is discarded. references/update.md is explicit that new corpus material gets folded in with a fresh held-out slice, and that full re-extraction is right in exactly one case, a contaminated corpus, which this is not. THE SHARP ASSERTION IS THE SHAPE OF THE FIX, not the routing. `clave` sits in VOICE.md as an exception WITH a proof quote, because a previous extraction already got it wrong in the other direction and VOICE_PROFILE.md records that under known errors. The complaint is about density, not about the word, so deleting the exception re-commits the error the profile is carrying a note about; the right fix is to move it into 'Con tope, no prohibidas', which the fixture already populates with `sin duda` so the shape is visible without the prompt priming it. ON GRADING THE ABLATION: the two routing assertions are with-only indicators — a baseline has no mode table and no references/ directory, so it cannot fail them and the delta on them is meaningless. Do not average them into a baseline pass rate. The rest of the assertions are genuinely comparable: nothing stops a baseline from capping rather than deleting, writing a regression case, or appending to the known-errors list, and whether it does is the real result.
assertions: Routes to `update`: loads references/update.md. It does NOT load references/init.md and does not begin a corpus extraction, a re-analysis of the corpus, or any of the three passes. WITH-ONLY INDICATOR — a no-skill baseline has no modes and cannot fail this; score it as a plugin-fired signal, not as part of the delta.

Resolves the profile itself and names where it found it: the project-local `.write-like-me/` in the working directory, stating the resolution rule. The prompt does not say where the profile is and a run that asks instead of resolving has not read the skill's first section.

Runs or reads the existing regression suite (regression/casos.md, cases C1-C3) BEFORE editing the profile, as references/update.md orders, rather than editing first and testing after. WITH-ONLY INDICATOR.

Does not delete `clave` from the exceptions table in VOICE.md §1. The complaint is about density, not about the word: the correct fix moves it to 'Con tope, no prohibidas' with a per-piece count, and its proof quote survives somewhere in the file. A run that strips the exception has re-committed the error VOICE_PROFILE.md already records under 'Errores conocidos de la extracción'.

Edits section 1 of VOICE.md and leaves the other sections alone. Diff the run's VOICE.md against ~/Projects/personal/agents/skills/write-like-me/evals/fixtures/perfil-de-prueba/VOICE.md: sections 2, 3, 4 and 5 must be byte-identical. The whole fix fits in §1, so there is no legitimate reason for them to move. This fails on a wholesale rewrite of the file even when the rewritten file is good — `update` is the cheap path precisely because it touches one section, and a run that regenerates the profile has done an extraction with extra steps.

Adds a case to regression/casos.md carrying the author's complaint in her own words plus the corrected behaviour, and the existing cases C1, C2 and C3 are all still present. A fix with no case silently regresses; a suite that quietly loses cases reports health forever.
Appends an entry to 'Errores conocidos de la extracción' in VOICE_PROFILE.md rather than replacing the two entries already there or creating the section fresh.
Tells the author which file and which section it changed, explicitly. They own the profile and a silent edit to it is worse than no edit.

Does not act on 'I've written a fair bit since we set this thing up' by starting an extraction or by folding unseen material into the profile. Either it sets the offer aside, or it proposes folding the new material in AND says a fresh slice must be held out before any of it is analysed.

Does not modify, create or delete any file under ~/.write-like-me/, or under ~/Projects/personal/agents/skills/write-like-me/evals/fixtures/. The run works on its own copy. A run that wrote to the home profile fails this regardless of the quality of what it wrote: that profile's regression cases hold the author's own verdicts and a spent held-out set, and overwriting them is unrecoverable.

evals.name: Mode routing - review is a critique, not a rewrite
evals.setup: Same fixture as eval 4 and the same copy-don't-symlink rule: `cp -R ~/Projects/personal/agents/skills/write-like-me/evals/fixtures/perfil-de-prueba "$RUN_DIR/.write-like-me"`, run with $RUN_DIR as the working directory, and say nothing to the run about where the profile is. This eval must NOT write to the profile at all, so the fixture copy doubles as the check: if the run's `.write-like-me/` differs from the fixture at the end, the run failed regardless of what its review said.
evals.prompt:
This is going out in the newsletter on Thursday. Tell me what in it doesn't sound like me, and don't touch it — I want to make the calls myself.

---

En un mundo cada vez más digitalizado, la gestión documental se ha convertido en uno de los grandes retos de las pequeñas asesorías.

Cabe destacar que la mayoría de los despachos siguen trabajando con carpetas compartidas sin ningún criterio de nombrado. Hemos preparado una guía para ayudarte a ordenarlas y creemos que te va a resultar útil.

Hay quien dice que con buscar por contenido basta y no hace falta ordenar nada. El argumento es potente y por eso da pereza rebatirlo, pero el buscador no te dice cuál de las cuatro versiones es la buena.

En resumen, ordenar la documentación es una inversión que merece la pena y el futuro de la gestión documental en el sector es prometedor.
evals.expected_output: The other half of the routing gap. SKILL.md's own framing is that handing a rewritten text to someone who asked for a critique is the most expensive of the four mode mistakes, because they lose the decision, and this prompt closes the ambiguity deliberately ('don't touch it') so the eval grades the review branch rather than the ask branch. Unlike eval 4 this one has a real baseline delta: a run with no skill, handed a draft and asked what's wrong with it, very plausibly returns an improved draft. THE PLANTS. Four violations, each mapping to a named section of the fixture's VOICE.md: (1) 'En un mundo cada vez más digitalizado...' — a scene-setting sector opening, where §4 Aperturas says dato concreto, fecha o cifra, never escena; (2) 'Cabe destacar que' — the strongest single marker in assets/es/llm-isms.md; (3) 'Hemos preparado... creemos' — first-person plural in a signed piece, banned outright in §1; (4) 'En resumen... el futuro... es prometedor' — summary plus uplift, where §4 Cierres says the last line is a decision or a question. AND ONE DECOY: 'El argumento es potente y por eso da pereza rebatirlo' is almost verbatim the proof quote that earns `potente` its place in §1's exceptions table. `potente` is on the generic ban list; a run that flags it has applied the generic list without filtering it through the profile, which is the failure that makes a voice skill actively worse than no skill. The piece also carries no concrete datum anywhere, which §3 makes the author's characteristic failure, so MISSING_PATTERN is available and a review that only walks the ban list will miss it.
assertions: Delivers a critique and no rewritten text. No corrected version of the piece, no rewritten sentences offered 'as an example', no before/after pairs built from this text. This fails on any line of replacement prose for the draft, however it is framed. The strongest single signal that the mode table was read and applied.

Returns line-level findings, each carrying a label from the skill's taxonomy (TOO_FORMAL, TOO_CASUAL, WRONG_WORD, LLM_ISM, NOT_ME, MISSING_PATTERN), a reason, and the section of VOICE.md that covers it — rather than prose commentary with no labels and no section references.
Catches the scene-setting opening ('En un mundo cada vez más digitalizado...') and ties it to §4 Aperturas, which requires a concrete datum, date or figure in the first sentence.
Catches 'Cabe destacar que' as an LLM-ism.
Catches the first-person plural in a signed piece ('Hemos preparado', 'creemos') and ties it to §1, which bans it outright for this author.
Catches the summary-plus-uplift close ('En resumen... el futuro... es prometedor') and ties it to §4 Cierres, which requires a decision or a direct question.

Does NOT flag `potente`. It is on the generic Spanish ban list and it is in §1's exceptions table with a proof quote that this sentence nearly reproduces. Flagging it fails the assertion outright: the skill's rule is to filter the generic lists through VOICE.md's exceptions before applying them, and stripping an author's own word makes the output worse, not safer.

Names at least one MISSING_PATTERN: the draft asserts throughout and never lands a figure, a date or a named case, which §3 identifies as this author's characteristic failure. A review that only walks the ban list finds four tells and misses the one thing wrong with the piece as a whole.

Loads the profile for `review` — VOICE.md, VOICE_PROFILE.md and the regression cases — and does not load references/init.md or references/update.md. WITH-ONLY INDICATOR: a baseline has neither file and cannot fail this.

Leaves the profile untouched. Diff the run's `.write-like-me/` against ~/Projects/personal/agents/skills/write-like-me/evals/fixtures/perfil-de-prueba/: every file must be byte-identical. `review` reads the profile; a review that edits it has silently run `update` on the author's behalf.
Does not modify, create or delete any file under ~/.write-like-me/, or under ~/Projects/personal/agents/skills/write-like-me/evals/fixtures/.
